translation: Two other small photos with scalloped edges, likely taken the same year, show the same child, but smaller in a dress with frills and puffed sleeves.
In the first one, she snuggles impishly against a woman of massive stature in a single-piece dress with wide stripes, her hair done up into large rolls.
In the second image, she raises her left fist while her right is held by a tall man dressed in a light jacket and pleated trousers striking an insouciant pose.
Both photos were taken on the same day beside a small wall adorned with flowers atop it on paved courtyard.
Above their heads runs lines of laundry from which one clothespin remains hanging.
Another photo, signed by the same photographer but on more ordinary paper and without the gold border likely intended for the same family distribution, shows a little girl of about four years old.
She seems serious, almost sad despite her plump and round face beneath short hair, parted in the middle and held back with barrettes from which ribbons are attached like butterflies.
Her left hand rests on the same carved table, fully visible in Louis XVI style.
She appears swollen in her bodice; her suspender skirt is hiked up at the front because of a protruding belly—perhaps a sign of rickets (circa 1944).
The boys were proud to join the regiment, and everyone thought them handsome in their uniforms.
On the evening of conscription board, they would visit all the coffee shops to celebrate being recognized as real men.
Before joining the army, they were still seen as kids who weren't worth anything on both work and marriage market.
Afterwards, they could take a wife and start a family.
The uniform that they paraded around their neighborhood during leave imbued them with patriotic beauty and projected sacrifice.
The shadow of victorious warriors—of GIs—hovered around them.
The rough cloth of their jackets grazed when you went on tiptoe to kiss them confirmed a firm line between men's world and women's world.
Seeing them stirred feelings of heroism within you.

Under the changelessness, the last year's circus posters with a photo of Roger Lanzac, first communion pictures given to friends, Club des Chansonniers on Radio Luxembourg, days filled up with new desires.
On Sunday afternoons, people crowded around the storefront of the general electronics store watching television.
Cafes would invest in buying a set just to attract customers.
Alongside hillsides slithered motocross tracks and one could watch noisy vehicles go up and down all day long.
The growing impatience of commerce shaking up city routines with its new catchwords, "initiative", "dynamism".
Between the funfair and village fetes arose commercial fortnights as spring rites.
In downtown streets speakers blared encouragements to buy interrupted by songs from Annie Cordy and Eddie Constantine for chances to win a Simca car or dining room set.

Up on a platform at City Hall Square was an MC who had locals laughing at jokes by comedians Roger Nicolas and Jean Richard; he would round up competitors for music contests or Quiz Show just like on radio programmingseated in one corner wearing her crown was Commerce Queen atop her throne.
Goods seemed more attractive under festive garb people were heard saying "it changes" or "we shouldn't vegetate.
.. we become stupefied staying home".
But they only spoke of what they had seen, which could be revisited in eating and drinking.
They lacked the talent or conviction to speak of what they knew but had not witnessed.
Therefore, neither Jewish children boarding trains for Auschwitz, nor starved corpses gathered in the Warsaw ghetto each morning, nor the 10,000 degrees at Hiroshima were discussed.

This gave an impression that history lessons, documentaries, and films would later fail to dispel: neither crematoriums nor atomic bomb belonged to the same era as black market butter, alerts and trips to the cellar.
They drew comparisons with the previous war, the Great War, that of 1914, which had been won in blood and glory a war of men that the women at the table listened to with respect.
They spoke of Chemin des Dames and Verdun, about those affected by gas attacks, and about the bells on November 11th, 1918.
They named villages from which not a single child sent to the front had returned.
They contrasted soldiers in muddy trenches with prisoners from '40 who were warm and sheltered for five years without even having bombs dropped on their heads.
They debated heroism and tragedy.

The children didn't listen and hurried to leave the table as soon as they were given permission, taking advantage of the general goodwill on festive days to engage in forbidden games, jumping on beds and swinging upside down.
But they retained everything.

Aside from the fabulous time of which they wouldn't order the episodes for a long while the Debacle, the Exodus, the Occupation, D-Day, Victory they found their own unnamed era in which they were growing up rather dull.
They regretted not having been born or barely so when it was necessary to set off in cohorts on roads and sleep on straw like gypsies.
For this unexperienced period, there would always be persistent regret.
Others' memories instilled hidden nostalgia for this time that had barely missed them and hope for one day experiencing it.
The frenzy that had followed the Liberation was fading.
Now people thought only of going out and the world was full of desires to be satisfied immediately.
Everything that constituted a first since the war provoked a rush bananas, national lottery tickets, fireworks.

In entire neighborhoods, from grandmothers supported by their daughters to infants in prams, people would rush to fairs, torchlight processions or Bouglione's circus where they risked being trampled in the crush.
They came together en masse praying and singing on roadsides to welcome the statue of Our Lady of Boulogne and escort it for miles on its return journey.
Whether secular or religious, any occasion was good enough for them to be outside together as if they wanted to continue living collectively taking advantage of their newly regained freedoms.

On Sunday evenings buses returned from the seaside filled with boisterous youngsters in shorts singing at the tops of their voices perched on luggage racks on roofs; dogs ran free coupling openly in the middle of streets.
Family narrative and social narrative are one and the same.
The voices of the guests defined the spaces of youth: the countryside and farms where, from time immemorial, men had been labourers and girls maidservants;
factories where they had all encountered, frequented, and married each other;
small businesses accessed by the most ambitious.

They outlined histories devoid of personal events apart from births, marriages and mournings –save for regimental journeys to distant garrison townslives consumed by work, in all its harshness and weariness;
with threats posed by alcohol never far away.
School was a mythical backdrop: a brief golden age wherein the schoolmaster reigned godlike with his iron ruler used to strike knuckles.
Browned photographs with backs stained by all the fingers that had held them at other meals—a mix of coffee and grease melded into an indistinguishable color—were passed from hand to hand.
In the stiff and solemn newlyweds, the wedding guests arranged in several rows along a wall, one recognized neither one's parents nor anyone else.
It wasn't oneself either seen in the half-naked baby of indistinct sex on a cushion, but someone else—a creature belonging to a silent and inaccessible time.
